articles.title: Tears of the Kingdom Shrine Map and Locations
articles.summary: Use this map to find all 152 Shrines on the Sky and Surface.
articles.body:
The Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom Shrine Maps below shows all 152 locations of shrines in TOTK. These maps was created using the Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom Interactive map here . Each shrine, 120 of which can be found on the Surface, and 32 more in the Sky, contains a mini-dungeon of puzzles to solve and loot including at least one Treasure Chest and a Light of Blessing . There are no Shrines in the Depths but there are Lightroots to discover that act as fast travel points in the Depths similar to Shrines . We've created a TOTK Lightroots Locations Map here as well.

Tears of the Kingdom Shrine Map: Surface

All 32 Tears of the Kingdom Shrine Locations in the Sky. Click the image for the full map with Shrine names, puzzle solutions, and more.

All 120 Tears of the Kingdom Shrine Locations in the Sky. Click the image for the full map with Shrine names, puzzle solutions, and more.

Note that we also have a massive Shrine checklist and full guides for each in our TOTK: All Shrine Locations and Solutions page.

Here are some helpful filters to aid you in your search. Click on the below links and you will ONLY see one type of map marker.

See all 1000 Korok Seed locations on the map: Yes, there are 1000 Koroks now, and we have locations and mini guides for every one.

We've got the152 Lightroot locations here as well.

See all 151 Cave locations on the map : Looking for Bubbul Gems? Look no further!

See all 135 Armor locations on the map : Armor can seriously boost your stats, and it's hard to find! Here's everything you need.

See all 15 Skyview Towers on the map: Uncover your own map by reaching these towers. We'll show you how.

See all 15 Stable locations on the map: Horses are important, but so are the side quests stables offer!

See all 5 Great Fairy locations on the map : Upgrade your armor at a Great Fairy!

Samuel Claiborn is IGN's managing editor and a fixes/breaks ancient arcade and pinball machines in his garage. TCELES B HSUP to follow him @Samuel_IGN on Twitter.

articles.title: Nintendo Switch 2 review: exactly good enough
articles.summary: The Nintendo Switch 2 launched on June 5th alongside Mario Kart World, and it offers a welcome, if predictable, update to the original.
articles.body: The first Switch was such a hit that Nintendo decided not to mess with a good thing. Instead of releasing a successor that feels like a generational leap or a pivot in a new direction, it’s following up the hugely successful original with the Switch 2 — a welcome upgrade that largely sticks to the formula. It looks about the same, works about the same, and plays most of the same games. It’s the Switch, just better. Nintendo’s bet is that it doesn’t have to wow people all over again, and so it made a sequel that’s only as good as it needs to be. After spending a week with the new console, I’ve realized that good enough is exactly what the Switch needed. A refined (and bigger) Nintendo Switch Fundamentally, the concept of the Switch hasn’t changed. It’s still a tablet with a split controller stuck on either side, with a dock that connects to your television. But the idea has been refined. The Switch 2 is much bigger, for one thing. It now has a 7.9-inch LCD panel, up from the original’s 6.2 inches, making it great for playing text-heavy games. It also means the entire device has become larger as a result, now weighing in at a comparatively hefty 1.18 pounds with the controllers attached. The larger size hasn’t bothered me, though your mileage may vary. My 12-year-old keeps stealing it to play Pokémon and hasn’t complained. But she’ll do anything for more screentime. [Product: Nintendo Switch 2 | There are some other nice upgrades. Like the most recent OLED model of the original Switch, the Switch 2 has a kickstand that can prop the system up at a wide range of angles, and the updated version feels a little sturdier to me, making it great for playing in tabletop mode. It’s a huge improvement over the original Switch’s flimsy kickstand. The Switch 2 also adds a second USB-C port to the top of the console, which enables you to plug in a webcam for online play. It’s handy for attaching a charger or battery pack whichever way is most convenient, too. What you get with that larger and heavier device is games that look and run better. The handheld’s screen has a 1920 x 1080 resolution, which supports HDR10 and VRR up to 120Hz. It’s bright and crisp, and games look a lot smoother thanks to the higher refresh rate. But I do miss the more vibrant OLED display of the most recent iteration of the original Switch, which featured deeper blacks and more contrast-y images. The new screen is a huge leap from the original, but it isn’t an all-around improvement if you’ve been using the OLED for a while. The story is different when connected to your TV: the Switch 2 can finally output at 4K, with support for HDR10. You’ll need to play supported games to really take advantage of this, but it’s immediately noticeable how much crisper everything from text to gameplay is. HDR promises to make games more vibrant, though there doesn’t seem to be a standout game to show this off just yet. [Image: Games are bigger this generation, too. Nintendo has increased the internal storage size to 256GB, but you’ll need to be diligent with how you use it; Cyberpunk 2077, for example, takes up 59GB on its own. Expanding that storage means buying a new and relatively expensive microSD Express card; your old microSD cards won’t work. More annoying is that the battery life is worse than the original Switch. Nintendo estimates between two and six and a half hours of gameplay on a single charge, and I found my device dying around the lower end of that spectrum, especially when playing more intensive games like Cyberpunk. That’s not a great sign for the future if the Switch 2 continues to get more demanding games. Some of this owes to the fact that this is simply a much more capable console. It’s built around a new Nvidia chip, custom designed for the Switch 2, and offering modern features like DLSS and ray tracing. There’s more RAM. The internal storage is faster. This is why the Switch 2 is able to run a game as demanding as Cyberpunk; it’s also why the Switch 2’s battery might die after a short two-hour stint. The Switch 2 also has slightly redesigned Joy-Con controllers. They’re functionally mostly the same, but bigger and with a few small upgrades, like more subtle vibrations. They connect via magnets now, which are less fiddly than the previous rail design. Nintendo says that the joysticks have been redesigned, too, but they still aren’t using anti-drift Hall effect sensors. That means there’s a chance owners will once again be dealing with the dreaded Joy-Con drift that plagued the original Switch. As similar as they are, the Joy-Con also introduces some of the truly new elements of the Switch 2. To start, the right Joy-Con has an all-new button dedicated entirely to Nintendo’s GameChat social features. Chatting with friends while playing games isn’t a new concept, but Nintendo has finally made it not only a core but a relatively painless part of its user experience. You simply pull up the app, and you can see what friends are online and what they’re playing. For the most part, it works as advertised. It’s easy to connect, voices come in clear through the Switch 2’s built-in mic, and video looks fine over the USB camera from Nintendo, which is sold separately. (The Switch 2 also supports an unclear number of third-party webcams.) This is a huge upgrade over Nintendo’s old way of doing things, where you needed to download a separate Nintendo Switch Online app onto your phone and use that secondary device to chat. [Media: The one flaw I’ve noticed with the new system is that screensharing — in which, for instance, four people can share their gameplay in Mario Kart World while they race against each other — looks choppy and ugly, to the point that I stopped using it. The redesigned Joy-Con controllers also introduce a new control option. By turning the Joy-Con on its side and placing it down on a flat surface, you’re able to use it like a mouse. Unfortunately, the Switch 2 doesn’t come with a next-gen version of Mario Paint to show all the mouse clicking possibilities, but I spent some time with the Switch 2 update of Civilization VII to test it out. And while it took some getting used to, I found the Switch 2’s mouse controls worked surprisingly well. This may not be as true in a twitchy first-person shooter where every millimeter matters, but for turn-based strategy, the mouse was a big improvement over a standard controller layout. In a nice touch, using the mouse is seamless; you don’t choose the option from a menu, you simply turn the Joy-Con on its side, place it down, and it begins mouse mode. This makes it easy to swap between control options on the fly. You also don’t need to use the mouse on a completely flat surface like a table or desk. I was able to play Civ just fine moving the Joy-Con around on my thigh. However, it wasn’t particularly comfortable to play that way for extended periods. So it’s hard to see it as something I’ll use often. So yes, the Switch 2 is exactly what it sounds like hardware-wise: it takes a winning concept and improves on it in subtle ways, and mostly doesn’t mess with what already worked. None of the changes are a huge leap, nor are any of the issues dealbreakers. A launch lineup that mixes old and new Of course, the most important aspect of any system is its games. And the launch lineup for the Switch 2 is a combination of new titles that take advantage of the more powerful hardware and older games that have been updated and are noticeably better compared to the original Switch versions. The best showcase for the console at launch is Mario Kart World. It expands upon its predecessor in ways that Nintendo says weren’t possible on the original Switch. The game takes place in a large, connected open world and doubles the number of racers from 12 to 24. It’s bigger, more ambitious, and more chaotic than any Mario Kart before it, and yet it also runs incredibly well on the Switch 2. It loads fast and the frame rate holds up, even when playing four-player split-screen, which introduces a frankly absurd number of explosions and crashes on your TV at any given moment. Outside of that, though, the first-party lineup is surprisingly thin. An impressive-looking Donkey Kong game is coming, but it doesn’t launch until July, so the only other Nintendo-made release is Nintendo Switch 2 Welcome Tour, an extremely drab collection of minigames and quizzes designed to teach you about the new console. It’s a nice idea, but the $10 collection is missing the Nintendo charm that can even make folding cardboard into a fun experience. [Image: That doesn’t mean there isn’t anything to play right now, though. There are just a few brand-new games. Many of the highlights of the Switch 2’s launch lineup are games that already exist on other platforms, but were likely too technically demanding for the original Switch. These include the likes of Cyberpunk 2077, Street Fighter 6, and Yakuza 0, all of which look good, run smoothly, and load quickly. The new handheld is not as powerful as other current-generation consoles, let alone a high-end PC, but it’s still pretty remarkable being able to take Night City with you wherever you go, and have it feel good to play, instead of just fine. Two of my favorite launch games take advantage of one of the Switch 2’s best features. Called GameShare, it lets you play select multiplayer games with anyone else nearby with a Switch 2 or original Switch, and it requires only one copy of the game. It’s not perfect — the second player is essentially streaming the game, and so the visual quality can dip at times — but it is a very fun way to enjoy co-op games that require a lot of coordination. I used it to play through a chunk of Split Fiction with my wife, and a few hours of Survival Kids with my, uh, kids, and it was a great alternative to couch co-op. We simply sat near each other, barking orders on what needed to be done next. While the core launch lineup may be lacking, there are a lot of games that have been updated in a significant way to support the Switch 2. Some of these are paid upgrades; I dropped $10 to be able to use those mouse controls in Civ, and it’ll cost you the same to get a much smoother and faster-loading version of Breath of the Wild or Tears of the Kingdom. These titles don’t look radically different, but they’re obviously sharper and running smoother; the faster loading times in Zelda may be worth the price of the upgrade alone. Many of the free upgrades are just as impressive. I’ve been especially struck by games I’ve already played for hundreds of hours — Fortnite and No Man’s Sky — both of which struggled mightily on the original Switch. But on the Switch 2 they look like and play like, well, modern games. Actually, my favorite launch games might be the oldest of all. One of the benefits for Nintendo Switch Online subscribers on the Switch 2 is the addition of GameCube games. To start, there are only three titles, but they’re excellent ones: The Legend of Zelda: The Wind Waker, Soulcalibur II (with Link as a playable fighter!), and F-Zero GX. It’s not exactly impressive that a sci-fi racer from 2003 plays fast and smooth on a modern console, but it’s still a nice bonus. And the GameCube has plenty of heavy hitters that will surely round out the service in the coming months. (Mario Kart: Double Dash, please.) [Image: A new generation that feels much like the last In 2017, there was nothing like the Nintendo Switch. At a time when dedicated handheld gaming devices had seemingly given way to smartphones, and the PS4 and Xbox One era was in full swing, here came Nintendo with an underpowered tablet that doubled as a home console in a way that was simple and intuitive. It proved to be such a success that it revitalized the company into a growing entertainment powerhouse. But eight years later, there’s a lot like the Nintendo Switch 2. The original spearheaded a resurgence in portable gaming thanks to the likes of Valve, Sony, and Xbox, and even upstarts like Panic and Analogue. The Switch 2 not only has to compete with its predecessor, but also a maturing market of modern handhelds. The Switch 2 doesn’t feel like the kind of generational leap typically associated with a new platform. When you put all of its features together — the larger display, more powerful internals, better social and sharing features, and more flexible control options — you are left with a device that is markedly better than its predecessor, but is still a step behind the latest PC handhelds in terms of pure horsepower and available games. But even with real competition this time around, Nintendo is still operating largely in its own sphere. And it turns out good enough is more than good enough when you also have the biggest Mario Kart to date.

articles.title: Intel’s first handheld gaming chip is the Arc G3, and this Acer is using it
articles.summary: And Acer’s first handheld will use it.
articles.body: Intel is barely in the handheld gaming PC space — but that might be about to change. After the embarrassment that was the first MSI Claw and the excellent MSI Claw 8 AI Plus that followed it, Intel said it would create custom handheld gaming chips. Today, it’s formally announcing them as the Arc G3 and Arc G3 Extreme. There’s a lot we don’t know about the chips, but Intel’s confirming today that the Panther Lake variant contains two fewer CPU cores than Intel’s Panther Lake laptop chips, but feature a full compliment of Xe3 GPU cores to run games. (They have 2 P-cores, 8 E-eores, and 4 LP E-cores, plus up to 12 Xe3 graphics cores in total.) [Image: Intel will support them with day-0 graphics driver updates as new games come out, and precompiled shaders so you don’t have as much stutter or load time in games, it claims. And, they’ll feature in at least three handhelds: the leaked MSI Claw 8 EX AI Plus, the just-announced OneXPlayer 3 with detachable controllers coming in June, and the just-announced Acer Predator Atlas 8 — which just might wind up being Acer’s first handheld after the Acer Nitro Blaze 7, 8, and gigantic 11 went MIA. [Image: The Predator Atlas 8, with dedicated Xbox Game Bar and “PredatorSense” buttons. The new Atlas 8 will come in at least two variants, one with an Intel Arc G3 Extreme and its Arc B390 graphics with 12 Xe3 GPU cores, and one with an Intel Arc G3 and the Arc B370 with 10 Xe3 cores instead. Each is paired with 24GB of LPDDR5x RAM at 7467 MT/s, and cooled by “the first metal fan in a handheld” with 89 blades and a claimed 10 percent airflow increase over the competition. The handheld will weigh around 810 grams (1.79lb) with a large 80Wh battery, or 770 grams (1.7lb) with an above-average 60Wh battery — presumably the higher end model comes with the bigger battery, like competing handhelds do. [Image: All the ports are up on top. The 8-inch screen sounds above average, too. It’s a 1920 x 1200 IPS panel at 16:10 aspect ratio, in a native landscape arrangement, with 500 nits of brightness and 48-120Hz variable refresh rate, covered in Gorilla Glass Victus with Corning’s DXC anti-glare coating with 100 percent sRGB and 77 percent Adobe RGB coverage. You won’t find magnetic Hall effect or TMR joysticks here, just carbon film ones that might eventually drift, but it does have Hall effect triggers with adjustable hair-trigger stops, two back buttons, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button. It’ll come with Windows 11 and Xbox Mode on up to a 1TB PCIe 4.0 SSD of the full-length M.2 2280 variety. While we haven’t held it yet, the spec sheet shows it’s roughly an inch thick (28.5mm) at its thinnest point and over two inches thick (58.37mm) at the grips. [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: [Image: And being an Intel platform, it comes with two Thunderbolt 4 ports (supporting 65W USB-C charging) and Intel’s flavor of Wi-Fi 7, as well as a UHS-II microSD card reader and 3.5mm headset jack. The company’s not talking battery life or price just yet, but it’s planning to launch the Atlas 8 in October. Retailer leaks suggest these handhelds could be quite pricey. Unfortunately, that seems to be the way of all handhelds these days: The Steam Deck got a huge price hike just yesterday. Update, May 28th: Added more info from Intel and OneXPlayer, including confirmation of two more handhelds.

articles.title: Black Myth: Zhong Kui Doesn’t Look as Epic as Wukong – and That’s Great
articles.summary: Black Myth: Zhong Kui looks more grounded than the epic myth that Black Myth: Wukong told, and I think it'll be more ambitious with its story because of that.
articles.body:
This is an IGN opinion piece from writer Tim Brinkhof, who loves challenging video games and has bested all of Black Myth: Wukong’s bosses (except Erlang , who continues to stand in the way of ultimate victory).

Black Myth: Zhong Kui is still years away. But if the recently released gameplay trailer provides an accurate impression of the final product, it seems we should expect the game to be a lot less epic than its predecessor, Black Myth: Wukong . As someone who adored the mythological scale and scope of developer Game Science’s triple-A debut, Zhong Kui’s grittier, muddier, more grounded approach initially struck me as disappointing. However, the more I think about it, the more I like it.

Based on many of the comments posted below the trailer, people largely seem pretty excited for Black Myth: Zhong Kui, which switches out Monkey King Sun Wukong for another beloved character from Chinese folklore, a demon hunter known as the “King of Ghosts.” But while I agree that the graphics look as stunning as ever and the combat – now featuring a welcome parrying mechanic – promises plenty of fun, the main thought that initially came to mind after watching the trailer was: “Wait…is that all?”

If this were any other developer, my expectations would be more than satisfied. But compared to Wukong – a game which, despite all odds, proved to be even better than I had dared to dream – Game Science’s upcoming project initially seems a little underwhelming. Where early gameplay footage for Wukong showcased an almost dizzying variety of stunning natural environments and architecture – from sun-drenched deserts to towering pagodas engulfed – most of the Zhong Kui trailer takes place inside a grey, dreary forest almost completely devoid of interesting landmarks. We don’t see our new protagonist transforming into animals, or ride a cloud, or face foes the size of skyscrapers, and the one boss fight shown in full – against a large, winged figure with a sword – isn’t quite as spectacular as the battle against Lingxuzi, the giant, bipedal wolf from the opening of Wukong.

That’s not to say that this project won’t continue the lineage Wukong started. Zhong Kui kicks some yaoguai butt here and there, and it’s clear that this is going to be a terrific action game. But the top and, in particular, tail of this extended first look showcases a game with what appears to be a slightly different ambition. We see Zhong Kui fishing, building a boat, and playing a musical instrument with a skeleton band. A little man bathes in a soup bowl, among numerous other small and rather silly interactions. It’s not exactly the kind of stuff that proves the sword-clashing credentials of your upcoming action game.

But what if action isn’t the point? While the original gameplay trailer for Wukong tried to awe and impress, Game Science’s first look at Zhong Kui seems like it wants to charm and intrigue. Its focus is not on boss battles or level design, but story and character, both of which appear to play a much more central role than they did in the developer’s previous project – and that’s pretty exciting.

As much as I loved its grandiose opening cutscene, the final boss fights against Wukong and Erlang, and pretty much every foe I fought in between, the thing about Wukong that ultimately stayed with me wasn’t the battles, but the ideas and emotions explored through its surprisingly touching narrative. More surprising than the quality of the gameplay or the length of the game itself was the fact that Game Science managed to craft a story which genuinely does its hallowed source material a bit of justice. The game functions not as an adaptation of Journey to the West so much as a sequel, picking up where the classic novel leaves off and building on this foundation in effective and thought-provoking ways.

Rather than leaning on nostalgia for the novel – and the hugely popular 1986 TV show whose iconic music inspired the game’s soundtrack – Wukong stands on its own legs, exploring themes of selfhood, freedom, and enlightenment that have resonated with ordinary players and scholars of Chinese history alike. The former see in Game Science’s Wukong a figure not unlike One Piece’s Monkey D. Luffy (the name, in case you didn’t know, is not a coincidence): someone who inspires them to persevere, live authentically, and trust in their own innate strength, while the latter have, among other interpretations, viewed the game as a metaphor for confronting China’s collective traumas.

I’d even go as far as to argue Wukong’s story and characters made up for its at times lackluster design. Various sections which were downright frustrating to play through on a gameplay level – like the mud-soaked fight against a possessed Pigsy in Chapter Four – were made bearable and, indeed, memorable because they occurred in points of the narrative which evoked feelings of despair and loss.

All of this is a roundabout way of saying that Wukong moved and made you think as much as it wowed and excited – and that, should Zhong Kui move more in the direction of the former at the expense of the latter, we might be in yet for another unexpected treat.

It is of course possible that the final game won’t be as light on spectacle as the footage suggests. Wukong is said to have been in development for more than six years, and since Game Science has yet to announce a release date for Zhong Kui, the developers may be saving the biggest surprises for later. Then again, that’s not really Game Science’s MO. At least, it hasn’t been up to this point. Against almost everyone’s expectations, the trailers for Wukong turned out to be a faithful reflection of the final game’s content and quality. As such, it’s not unreasonable to expect Zhong Kui to offer what this early footage indicates: a less grand, more story-driven experience.

Another reason why I expect Game Science to move into this direction is because doing so would be completely antithetical to how games are being made in the West. Over here, where profit incentives often interfere with talent and vision, triple-A franchises tend to get bigger with each installment, even though few would say that bigger automatically equals better.

For many non-Chinese players, Wukong was a breath of fresh air. Not just because it was produced in a country that hadn’t previously been known for its games – at least, not of this kind – but also because its unique and outspoken personality contrasted so sharply with the state of the gaming industry at large, where rampant commercialization and monetization has left many blockbuster titles feeling rather soulless.

On the same day Game Science released the gameplay trailer for Zhong Kui, its founder, Feng Ji, uploaded a post on his Weibo account in which he shared the company’s 10 development principles. The first of these principles – a translation of which can be found on Reddit – essentially states that the developers strive to make the kinds of games they want to play themselves, rather than chasing consumer trends. Regardless of how Black Myth: Zhong Kui will turn out, this philosophy promises a game that may be a little different from its predecessor, but no less lovingly put together.

Tim Brinkhof is a freelance writer specializing in art and history. After studying journalism at NYU, he has gone on to write for Vox, Vulture, Slate, Polygon, GQ, Esquire and more.

articles.title: Acer’s new concept hardware is a gaming handheld with a keyboard
articles.summary: Project DualPlay Mini has a swiveling screen and a flip-out keyboard.
articles.body: For the last few years, PC gamers on the go have had a choice: Buy a gaming laptop, or pick up one of the many Steam Deck–inspired handhelds that are a fraction of the size but a lot less versatile. Acer’s latest concept device, Project DualPlay Mini, is an attempt to upend that dichotomy by sticking a keyboard in a handheld. The DualPlay Mini is first and foremost a Windows gaming handheld, cut from the same cloth as Acer’s existing Predator Atlas 8 (which is being joined this week by a new 7-inch model). In its default configuration, the handheld’s screen is flanked by analog sticks, a D-pad, and Xbox-style ABXY face buttons, plus two triggers on each shoulder. But the DualPlay Mini’s “flip-and-swivel design” allows you to flip the device open and swivel the screen round to instead line it up with a compact, backlit mini keyboard. [Image: [Image: With a dinky little 8-inch screen, I’m not sure the DualPlay Mini would ever become anyone’s primary work device, unless they intended to make heavy use of its ability to connect to an external screen. But it might be just enough to make it a useful backup option while traveling, letting you bring one device instead of two. The option to play keyboard-friendly PC games on a device the size of a Steam Deck is an obvious appeal too. Since the DualPlay Mini is strictly a concept, with no plans for a retail release, Acer hasn’t gone into much detail on the specs inside it so far. It’s powered by an Intel chip and uses a similar dual-fan cooling design to the Predator Atlas 8 — with one metal fan and one plastic — though the blades on the metal element are thinner than before. A pair of USB-C ports sit on the back, with Thunderbolt support on one. [Image: [Image: [Image: It’s unclear if Acer will ever release a real product with anything like the DualPlay Mini’s design, but I’ll be seeing all of Acer’s new IFA hardware this week, and I’m hoping for a chance to get my hands on the DualPlay Mini to see if the concept has legs.

articles.title: Pokémon Fans Think The Franchise's New TCG Movie Hides a Secret Mega Evolution
articles.summary: The reveal of upcoming movie Pokémon: Wild Card hid a brand new Mega Evolution in plain sight, fans believe.
articles.body:
The reveal of upcoming movie Pokémon: Wild Card hid a brand new Mega Evolution in plain sight, fans believe.

Over the weekend, the 2026 Pokémon World Championships included a flurry of new Pokémon announcements, including the first new Pokémon movie for seven years . Due to launch in theaters next year, Pokémon: Wild Card will feature a TCG player "battling and striving to be a champion", accompanied by a mysterious Mimikyu.

Of course, Mimikyu does not currently have a Mega Evolution — not in the series' original Pokémon X and Y batch of Megas, or in the fresh menagerie introduced last year via Pokémon Legends: Z-A. But there is something odd about the Mimikyu in that poster — do you see it?

Yes, the Mimikyu is glowing with rainbow-colored light — a very similar rainbow-colored light to the effect of Pokémon as Mega Energy, used to Mega Evolve. Is it a coincidence, or something more? And if we are about to see a Mega Mimikyu revealed, when could it debut in video game form?

One popular suggestion is that Mimikyu will evolve in next year's Pokémon Winds and Waves, the franchise's long-awaited 10th generation of games due to arrive exclusively for Nintendo Switch 2. With these games and Pokémon: Wild Card arriving around the same time, this would be a neat teaser — and certainly, anime movies and series have previously featured various Pokémon debuts before they're actually available in-game.

One other avenue for release could be via a final update to Pokémon Legends: Z-A , a game which focuses squarely on Mega Evolution. This would likely make more sense thematically, and there's been no suggestion that Winds and Waves will include Mega Evolution themselves. Indeed, as a new generation of games, the upcoming titles are more likely to feature their own regional mechanic (such as Gigantamax in Sword and Shield, or Terrestrialization in Scarlet/Violet).

Could Mega Mimikyu debut sooner rather than later in Legends: Z-A, as a way to tide fans over while news on Winds and Waves' launch window remains thin on the ground? Or could this all just be another one of Mimikyu's tricks? Fans seem convinced Mega Mimikyu is coming, either way.

Mega Mimikyu would be so goated and I would not be normal about it. I felt that it was such an obvious choice. Mega Mimikyu’s ability should restore disguise — 👑🤴🏻Spoopy🪦💀 (@Prince_Spoopy) September 1, 2026

For everything announced during the 2026 Pokémon World Championships and PokémonXP, check out our roundup . Pokémon: Wild Card may be the only feature-length movie announced, but another animated Pokémon project is making its way to screens in 2027. Pokémon Tales: The Misadventures of Sirfetch'd and Pichu was announced back in 2025, but news about the series streaming on DisneyXD and more was revealed during a panel at this year's PokémonXP .

articles.title: The amazing USB-C gadgets that play old Nintendo cartridges
articles.summary: The $60 Epilogue SN Operator and $50 GB Operator let you play, save, and backup real Super Nintendo and Game Boy games.
articles.body: Last week, I powered on a 26-year-old copy of Pokémon Pinball, one of the best Game Boy games ever made. My save file was no more. The Charmander I’d caught for my daughter, the high scores we’d set together… gone. Before flash memory, Nintendo cartridges used tiny watch batteries to save their games, and those batteries were never meant to last this long. But it’s not a huge deal, because I saved my family’s save file months ago. I backed it up with an Epilogue Operator, a device that connects your real Nintendo cartridges to Windows PCs, MacBooks, even a Steam Machine. [Media: The $50 GB Operator is a transparent trapezoidal cartridge reader that reads and writes to real Game Boy, Game Boy Color and Game Boy Advance cartridges over a USB-C cable; the company’s new $60 SN Operator does the same for Super Nintendo and Japanese Super Famicom titles. Epilogue’s also got a N64 version coming. They’re not just for backups! As you can see in my embedded video, these gadgets can play your carts, too. My Xbox Ally now takes Super Nintendo cartridges, my Steam Deck plays Game Boy carts, and my phone is a Game Boy Camera, because I attached an Epilogue Operator to each one. (Double-sided magnet rings and Mechanism mounts helped.) Technically, the SN Operator and GB Operator are just cartridge readers, there are no original Nintendo chips or FPGAs inside. When you play a game, your computer saves the ROM to your computer and plays it in an emulator. But Epilogue’s Playback software makes that easy — just plug in the reader, plug in the cart, hit play — and it casts a convincing illusion that you’re playing your games on actual carts. Plug one in, and your game pops up on screen. Whenever you save in the game, Epilogue should automatically save back to your cartridge as well. Whenever you yank a cart, the game instantly winks out. [Image: [Image: That last one’s a bit of a double-edged sword, because Epilogue’s Operators can be touchy about cartridge detection. They aren’t as forgiving as an actual Super Nintendo or Game Boy if your carts are slightly dirty or damaged. I’ve got Japanese copies of Bahamut Lagoon and Sailor Moon R that’ll quit mid-session if I nudge them wrong. But I love that I can write savegames to my cartridges: I can play a game on my PC, move the cartridge over to my Steam Deck, then pop it into an actual original Game Boy or Super Nintendo and pick up where I left off. If you don’t need to automatically write saves, you can even switch to an emulator core that offers RetroAchievements, plus optional creature comforts like saving anywhere in a game with save states, or the ability to rewind time and try that tricky jump once more. [Image: Super Nintendo on an Xbox Ally? Yep. Want to hear something especially nerdy? My family recently played Super Metroid on the Super Famicom Classic Edition that Nintendo released in 2017, and there’s actually a way to pull your savegames off of those emulator consoles, too. I converted and wrote that savegame to my actual Japanese Super Metroid cartridge, and now I’m playing that save on 30-year-old original Nintendo hardware. (Speaking of: did you know a Japanese copy of Super Metroid is downright affordable and entirely in English?) [Image: (I attached the SN Operator with a Mechanism mount and some right-angle USB-C adapters. I never had a Super Nintendo growing up, and I don’t have a working Super Scope light gun or SNES Mouse now. But the SN Operator is also helping me play amazing games like Metal Combat: Falcon’s Revenge and Mario Paint and share them with my kids, no crusty old peripherals necessary. There’s an option to let your PC mouse cursor emulate a light gun or mouse, and it was simple to map those to my Steam Controller’s gyroscope aiming. While you can do most if not all of these things by pairing emulators with other hardware, including the Open Source Cartridge Reader and a variety of Game Boy readers, Epilogue’s hardware is surprisingly high-quality considering its low cost, with attractive minimalist circuit boards clearly visible through classy polycarbonate. You know how we love our transparent gadgets around here. [Image: Here’s the back of the GB Operator. And Epilogue isn’t just riding on the coattails of emulator developers, either. While the hardware’s proprietary, the Romanian company contributes some money and some code to open source emulators. Co-founder Petru Sebastian Toader also tells me he built his software’s excellent new CRT filter himself, the company’s working on online multiplayer, and every single SN Operator has its clockspeed factory-calibrated using satellites so they can dump certain SNES games without errors. Epilogue’s also teamed up with the developers of Delta Emulator so you can plug real carts into your phone, and even built its own Flashback app if you want to turn your phone into a Game Boy Camera. [Image: The Operator’s 3D trapezoidal prism shape doesn’t exactly lend itself to portability, but I stuck a magnet ring to it just right. With all these amazing features, I just think Epilogue should be a little bit more upfront on its product pages about the compromises you need to make. You should know the limitations: the Operators don’t work with multi-game flashcarts, they don’t work with the Super Game Boy, and their heavily marketed “Counterfeit cartridge detection” has been very hit or miss in my tests, to the point I wouldn’t really trust it. The company advertises that it can turn your Game Boy Camera into a webcam, but it’s more of an OBS screen recording hack than I would have guessed. [Image: The GB Operator. And if you, like me, have original Game Boy cartridges with original batteries, it may be too late to save some of your saves by now. It’s far too late to pull Pokémon off second-gen games like Pokémon Gold, Silver and even Crystal, whose real-time clocks drained their backup batteries and might not have lasted more than a decade. As for first-gen Game Boy games, I pulled a Charmander off an original Pokémon Red cart last year, but even those carts are reaching their battery’s end of life. I have a 30-year-old copy of The Legend of Zelda: Link’s Awakening whose battery was working last month. Last week, I found its save, too, was gone. Thankfully, the GB Operator backed up my progress a few months ago. Now I just need to install a new battery, flash my save, and I’ll be back in business.

articles.title: Viral Gaming Toilet Chair Appears to Resurface Via Facebook Marketplace — Listed as in 'Used' Condition, for $500
articles.summary: A viral fan-made Fortnite toilet chair made infamous via TikTok has apparently resurfaced via Facebook Marketplace, with the item priced at $500 and listed as in "used" condition.
articles.body:
A viral fan-made Fortnite toilet chair made infamous via TikTok has apparently resurfaced via Facebook Marketplace, with the item priced at $500 and listed as in "used" condition.

The so-called "Battle Bucket" was the subject of a now-deleted 2023 TikTok video from user @usecodelitty200iq, who explained the home-made contraption was the reason he could "play Fortnite for so long without going to the bathroom."

The Battle Bucket is essentially a flip chair with a crude hole cut into the seat, and an orange five gallon Home Depot bucket underneath. A curved length of piping has also been placed at the front of the seat, arcing down into the bucket's base. On the back of the chair, a G Fuel sticker has been artfully placed.

"I call this the Fortnite Battle Bucket," @usecodelitty200iq described at the time. "It has two holes. One for going number one, and another for going number two," he continued, pointing to the pipe and seat hole in quick succession.

@xset The Battle Bucket Is CRAZY.. 😂 (TT:@/usecodelitty200iq) #foryoupage #foryou #fyp #trending #gaming #fortnite ♬ original sound - XSET

While the original video has now been removed, numerous examples of it remain online via reuploads. And now, the device itself appears to have resurfaced for real, via an X account that supposedly spotted it listed on Facebook marketplace. Certainly, the listing includes a high-quality photo of the Battle Bucket not part of the original video, suggesting whoever is behind it has access to the real thing.

"I've had this for a few years and used it almost daily," the listing reads. "Has been thoroughly cleaned and works beautifully." And then, one final note: "Real offers only! No lowballs I know what I got."

**USED** Battle Bucket ($500) pic.twitter.com/ff2nqoCN6t — insane facebook marketplace items (@insanemrktplace) August 31, 2026

**USED** Battle Bucket ($500) pic.twitter.com/ff2nqoCN6t

As a functioning replacement for going to the bathroom, or indeed a replacement for operating as a functional human being, this seems unlikely to raise $500. As a piece of internet history, well, it still seems unlikely to raise $500. And although the listing claims the viral chair has been cleaned, I'd still be worried of a different kind of viral issue when sitting down on it.

Here's hoping we hear more on the Fortnite Battle Bucket, if and when the sale proceeds. In the meantime, the internet has certainly been having its fun with the listing, with comments from various brands piling in.

"Powered by yours truly," wrote the official G Fuel social media account. "It's been an honor to serve you 🫡."

"Adding this to the list of banned items at LAN," wrote UK esports event organiser Epic.LAN.

I also enjoyed this oil painting of the Fortnite Battle Bucket, immortalizing its TikTok appearance forever:

I made an oil painting of the most insane Facebook marketplace find pic.twitter.com/rzkm4gPHoL — Cayde.wav (@caydeplanet) September 1, 2026

I made an oil painting of the most insane Facebook marketplace find pic.twitter.com/rzkm4gPHoL

Let us know if you're planning to bid on the item, or indeed if you become the, er, lucky owner.
